newsitem.title: FRANCE: Election forecast buoys France's centre-right.
newsitem.headline: Election forecast buoys France's centre-right.

text.p: France's ruling centre-right goes into the campaign for next month's parliamentary election buoyed by a survey predicting it will retain power with a large majority.

The poll -- the first since President Jacques Chirac called the election on Monday 10 months ahead of schedule -- foresaw the ruling coalition winning 332 seats in the National Assembly's to 222 for the combined left-wing opposition.
It held a huge 464-seat majority in the outgoing assembly.
The CSA poll appeared to back Chirac's daring gamble which France's EU partners see as a roll of the dice that could make or break Europe's plan for a single currency.

Unpopular Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe, undaunted by a survey showing his and Chirac's standing falling further, has promised an aggressive campaign to win the poll and lead a modernised France into the European economic and monetary union.

Juppe repeated Chirac's argument that the government needed renewed legitimacy to join the euro in time in 1999 and reform the state, cutting public spending and taxes and freeing business from over-regulation.
"France has nothing to fear but everything to gain from the euro, everything to gain from the Union, everything to gain from Europe," he said. "Let us be the motor of this great adventure."

The CSA poll said voters were split 44 to 44 percent over whether Chirac was right in calling the snap election and 57 percent were unconvinced by his statement that an early election was necessary with 81 percent seeing it as a political game.
Preaching unity to his often fractious coalition, Juppe presented a platform stressing continuation of current policies.

As a symbol of reconciliation, former prime minister Edouard Balladur who fought fellow-Gaullist Chirac in a fratricidal 1995 presidential election battle, was taken out of political isolation to attend his speech with the coalition leaders.

Ignoring Juppe's denials, the left-wing opposition accused Chirac of preparing a new turn of the austerity screw to meet the strict budget deficit criteria which the Maastricht Treaty's requires for entry to a single currency.
A senior government official told Reuters further austerity would be required in the autumn to meet the criteria.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin rejected a fresh bout of austerity and said that if the opposition won the election, he would negotiate a softening of the treaty's criteria.
"If we come to power next June, we will have almost a year to make proposals to our partners, particularly the Germans, on these issues," he told TF1 television.
Jospin challenged Juppe to a televised debate, and Juppe indicated he may accept it.

In a consequence of the early election, the government postponed by a month its biggest privatisation project, the sale of a minority stake in telecommunications giant France Telecom SA which was due to have been floated next month.
Jospin said he was against continuing privatisations and a Socialist government would not sell off France Telecom.

Financial markets, still jittery from uncertainty generated by the early poll, began a comeback on Tuesday. The franc and fixed income markets were stronger on the view the conservatives were likely to keep a majority. The stock market closed down 0.32 percent, its third consecutive drop.
